etymology: Hebrew Nadab (H5070) — "generous, willing, noble," from the root nadab ("to incite, offer voluntarily"). The same name was borne by Aaron's eldest son (Lev 10:1-2, killed for strange fire) and by this second king of Israel.
biblical_def: Nadab (c. 910 — 909 BC) was the second king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:25-31), son of Jeroboam I son of Nebat. His two-year reign was the entire duration of the Jeroboam dynasty after its founder. He continued in his father's golden-calf apostasy at Bethel and Dan, and was assassinated while besieging the Philistine city of Gibbethon by his military commander Baasha, who then proceeded to kill every male of Jeroboam's house in fulfillment of Ahijah the Shilonite's earlier prophecy (1 Kings 14:10-11). His brief reign is the first instance of the recurring divided-monarchy pattern: a king continues in Jeroboam's sin; the LORD's prophet-pronounced judgment falls; the dynasty is extinguished; the assassin becomes king and continues the same apostasy.
webster_summary: Second king of Israel (c. 910-909 BC); son of Jeroboam I; reigned 2 years; assassinated by Baasha at the siege of Gibbethon; all males of Jeroboam's house then killed in fulfillment of Ahijah's prophecy.
webster_full: NADAB, proper noun. Hebrew Nadab (H5070) — "generous, willing, noble."
Second king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 910-909 BC); son of Jeroboam I.
Two-year reign; continued the golden-calf apostasy; assassinated by Baasha at the siege of Gibbethon (1 Kings 15:27-28).
Distinct from Nadab the son of Aaron (Lev 10:1-2), killed for strange fire.
scriptures: And Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned over Israel two years. And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin.

And Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him; and Baasha smote him at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines... Even in the third year of Asa king of Judah did Baasha slay him, and reigned in his stead.
1 Kings 14:10
Therefore, behold, I will bring evil upon the house of Jeroboam, and will cut off from Jeroboam him that pisseth against the wall.
Leviticus 10:1-2
And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron... offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the LORD, and devoured them.
corruption_summary: Nadab is corrupted when his short reign is treated as merely a transitional curiosity rather than as the first instance of the recurring divided-monarchy coup-and-judgment pattern, or when his name is conflated with Aaron's son Nadab who died for strange fire.
corruption_paragraphs: Two different Nadabs. The name Nadab appears in Scripture for at least two important figures: Aaron's eldest son (Lev 10:1-2), who together with his brother Abihu was struck dead for offering strange fire in the wilderness tabernacle, and this second king of Israel (1 Kings 15:25). Popular Sunday-school treatment sometimes conflates them or treats Nadab-the-king as a footnote. They are entirely distinct figures separated by roughly five centuries; both share the irony that their name means 'willing/generous' yet both ended in divine judgment.

Transitional-king dismissal. Nadab's two-year reign is sometimes skipped in surveys of the divided monarchy. The Chronicler-style narrator in 1 Kings 15 highlights it precisely because it inaugurated the recurring pattern: a dynasty established by Jeroboam's choice to lead Israel into the golden-calf cult could not last more than one generation because the prophetic judgment had already been pronounced. The lesson is doctrinal-generational: covenant rejection produces dynastic destruction, however brief the second-generation reign.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nadab (H5070) — "generous, willing." The second king of Israel (c. 910-909 BC); son of Jeroboam I; assassinated by Baasha.

Continued his father's golden-calf apostasy; killed at the siege of Gibbethon.
His death and his family's extermination fulfilled Ahijah the Shilonite's prophecy against the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 14:10).

etymology: Hebrew Elah (H425) — "oak" or "terebinth tree." Multiple biblical figures bore this name; the king is distinct from the Valley of Elah (1 Sam 17:2) where David fought Goliath.
biblical_def: Elah (c. 886 — 885 BC) was the fourth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:8-14), son of Baasha and his only known successor. His two-year reign ended ignominiously: while his army was again besieging the Philistine city of Gibbethon (the same city where his father Baasha had assassinated his predecessor Nadab a generation earlier), Elah remained in Tirzah and drank himself into stupor at the house of his chamberlain Arza. His own chariot-commander Zimri broke into the house, killed him, and then systematically killed every male of Baasha's house, fulfilling the prophecy that Jehu son of Hanani had pronounced over his father (1 Kings 16:1-4). The Baasha dynasty ended exactly as the Jeroboam dynasty had: two kings, then extinction by coup. Elah is the canonical pattern-piece of how drunkenness and complacency end a dynasty already under prophetic judgment.
webster_summary: Fourth king of Israel (c. 886-885 BC); son of Baasha; reigned 2 years; drank himself into stupor in Tirzah while his army besieged Gibbethon; assassinated by his chariot-commander Zimri; all males of Baasha's house then killed.
webster_full: ELAH, proper noun. Hebrew Elah (H425) — "oak" or "terebinth."
Fourth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 886-885 BC); son of Baasha.
Two-year reign; assassinated by his chariot-commander Zimri while drunk at the house of Arza his chamberlain.
Distinct from the Valley of Elah (1 Sam 17:2), Esau's son Elah (Gen 36:41), and other minor figures of the same name.
scriptures: In the twenty and sixth year of Asa king of Judah began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah, two years. And his servant Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspired against him, as he was in Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza steward of his house in Tirzah. And Zimri went in and smote him, and killed him, in the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his stead.

And it came to pass, when [Zimri] began to reign, as soon as he sat on his throne, that he slew all the house of Baasha: he left him not one that pisseth against a wall... thus did Zimri destroy all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD.
Proverbs 23:29-32
Who hath woe? who hath sorrow?... they that tarry long at the wine... At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder.
1 Kings 16:1-4
Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha... Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha...
corruption_summary: Elah is corrupted when his drunken-stupor death is treated merely as a colorful narrative detail rather than as the canonical illustration of how complacency completes a prophetic judgment, or when the parallel between his death and his father Baasha's coup is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Drunkenness-as-colorful-detail. The detail in 1 Kings 16:9 that Elah was 'drinking himself drunk' when Zimri killed him is sometimes treated as the equivalent of historical color — an interesting Tirzah-palace anecdote. The narrator's framing is theological: the king of Israel under prophetic judgment was incapacitated by drink in the safety of a steward's house while his army fought at the front. The Chronicler's juxtaposition of drinking and dynastic destruction is the same warning the wisdom literature gives in Proverbs 23:29-35.

Parallel-pattern overlooked. Elah's death exactly parallels Nadab's: both killed by their successor at or near the same Philistine city of Gibbethon; both followed by the extinction of their entire male family; both fulfilling prior prophetic judgment (Ahijah for Jeroboam; Jehu son of Hanani for Baasha). The narrator wants the reader to feel the recurrence as the necessary pattern, not as bad luck. Dynasties built on continuing apostasy end in coup; the divided monarchy's history is the working-out of this principle.

The pattern repeats: Jeroboam I — Nadab — coup; Baasha — Elah — coup.

etymology: Hebrew Zimri (H2174); uncertain meaning, possibly "my song" or "my praise" (from zamar, "to sing, make music"). The same name was borne by the Simeonite man speared by Phinehas at Peor (Num 25:14).
biblical_def: Zimri (c. 885 BC, seven-day reign) was the fifth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:9-20), captain of half the chariots under Elah son of Baasha, whose coup against his master produced one of the shortest reigns in the entire Bible and one of its most dramatic ends. After assassinating Elah at Tirzah and killing every male of Baasha's house, Zimri took the throne; but when the army at Gibbethon heard the news they immediately proclaimed their general Omri king and marched on Tirzah. Within seven days Omri's forces had besieged the city; Zimri, seeing capture inevitable, went into the inner room of the king's palace and burned the palace down around himself rather than be taken (1 Kings 16:18). His name became a byword in Israel: when Jehu's revolt was approaching some seventy years later, Jezebel called to him from her window: "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" (2 Kings 9:31) — a sneering reference to the brief and disastrous fate of the previous master-killing coup-leader. His seven-day reign embodies one strand of the divided-monarchy pattern: usurpation without prophetic mandate ends quickly and badly.
webster_summary: Fifth king of Israel (c. 885 BC); chariot-commander under Elah; reigned only 7 days; burned the palace down around himself rather than be captured by Omri's army; became a byword for treacherous usurpation (Jezebel taunted Jehu: 'Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?').
webster_full: ZIMRI, proper noun. Hebrew Zimri (H2174); uncertain meaning, possibly "my song."
Fifth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885 BC); originally chariot-commander under Elah.
Reigned only 7 days; assassinated Elah, killed all of Baasha's house, then was besieged by Omri's army at Tirzah and burned the palace down around himself.
Distinct from Zimri the Simeonite speared by Phinehas at Peor (Num 25:14), and from Zimri son of Zerah (1 Chr 2:6).
scriptures: In the twenty and seventh year of Asa king of Judah did Zimri reign seven days in Tirzah... And it came to pass, when Zimri saw that the city was taken, that he went into the palace of the king's house, and burnt the king's house over him with fire, and died.
1 Kings 16:19
For his sins which he sinned in doing evil in the sight of the LORD, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did, to make Israel to sin.
2 Kings 9:31
And as Jehu entered in at the gate, [Jezebel] said, Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?
Proverbs 21:25-26
The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour. He coveteth greedily all the day long...
corruption_summary: Zimri is corrupted when his seven-day reign is treated as theatrical irrelevance rather than as the canonical example of usurpation-without-prophetic-mandate, or when Jezebel's later taunt is read as merely insulting Jehu without recognizing the doctrinal point her insult was making.
corruption_paragraphs: Seven-day-reign as theater. The dramatic detail of Zimri's suicide-by-arson is sometimes treated as the most memorable thing about him — a colorful Tirzah-palace scene rather than a doctrinal datum. The narrator's interest is theological: even after fulfilling the prior prophecy (the extermination of Baasha's house), Zimri's reign was illegitimate because no prophet had been sent to anoint him as king. He was the instrument of one judgment but possessed no mandate for his own dynasty. The seven-day collapse demonstrates the principle: God's instruments of judgment are not automatically God's chosen rulers.

Jezebel's taunt over-personalized. When Jehu came in his coup against the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9), Jezebel called from her window: 'Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?' (2 Kings 9:31). The taunt is often read as Jezebel's defiant personal insult — calling Jehu another fly-by-night usurper like Zimri seventy years earlier. The fuller doctrinal weight is that Jezebel may have been technically right about the parallel and entirely wrong about its meaning: Jehu, unlike Zimri, had been anointed by a prophet sent from Elisha (2 Kings 9:1-10). The same kind of coup with prophetic mandate became the longest northern dynasty (Jehu — Jehoahaz — Joash — Jeroboam II — Zachariah; ninety-plus years).

etymology: Hebrew Yehoachaz (H3059) — "Yahweh has grasped/seized." From Yah (the divine name) + achaz ("to grasp"). Distinct from Ahaz of Judah, whose shortened form is the same root.
biblical_def: Jehoahaz (c. 814 — 798 BC) was the eleventh king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 13:1-9), son of Jehu and second king of the Jehu dynasty, whose seventeen-year reign represents the lowest geopolitical point of the northern kingdom under Aramean pressure from Hazael of Damascus. The canonical record assigns him a mixed verdict: he did evil in the way of Jeroboam (the golden-calf cult continued) yet at the depth of Aramean oppression he 'besought the LORD' and the LORD heard him and gave Israel a deliverer (unnamed in 2 Kings 13:5; possibly the Assyrian king Adad-nirari III whose Damascus campaigns took pressure off Israel). His army was reduced by Hazael to a humiliating remnant: fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot, 'for the king of Syria had destroyed them, and had made them like the dust by threshing' (2 Kings 13:7). His name — 'Yahweh has grasped' — was reflected in the LORD's reluctant covenant compassion that prevented Israel's complete extinction during his reign. He was succeeded by his son Joash of Israel (Jehoash-of-Israel).
webster_summary: Eleventh king of Israel (c. 814-798 BC); son of Jehu; second king of the Jehu dynasty; reigned 17 years under Hazael of Aram's pressure; army reduced to remnant; besought the LORD and was given a deliverer (2 Kings 13:5).
webster_full: JEHOAHAZ, proper noun. Hebrew Yehoachaz (H3059) — "Yahweh has grasped." Distinct from the longer-form name of Ahaz of Judah.
Eleventh king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 814-798 BC); son of Jehu; second king of the Jehu dynasty.
17-year reign under intense Aramean pressure from Hazael of Damascus; army reduced to 50 horsemen, 10 chariots, 10,000 foot (2 Kings 13:7).
Besought the LORD in oppression; the LORD gave Israel a deliverer (possibly Adad-nirari III of Assyria; the text leaves the deliverer unnamed).
Distinct from Jehoahaz son of Josiah (later king of Judah, deposed by Pharaoh-Necho; 2 Kings 23:31-34).
scriptures: 2 Kings 13:2-4

And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD... And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria... And Jehoahaz besought the LORD, and the LORD hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel.
2 Kings 13:5
And the LORD gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians: and the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime.
2 Kings 13:7
Neither did he leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen; for the king of Syria had destroyed them, and had made them like the dust by threshing.

Many times did he deliver them; but they provoked him with their counsel... Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry: And he remembered for them his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his mercies.
corruption_summary: Jehoahaz is corrupted when his beseeching-the-LORD episode is treated as full repentance rather than as the partial cry-from-oppression it was, when the unnamed 'deliverer' is over-identified with one historical figure, or when he is confused with the later Judean Jehoahaz son of Josiah.
corruption_paragraphs: Beseeching as full repentance. 2 Kings 13:4 records that Jehoahaz 'besought the LORD' and the LORD heard him in the oppression. The chapter immediately makes clear this was not a covenant turning: 'Nevertheless they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who made Israel to sin' (2 Kings 13:6). The pattern is the typical biblical one: oppression produces a cry to Yahweh; Yahweh's covenant compassion sends relief; the people resume the apostasy that brought the oppression. Beseeching-without-turning is a recurring Israelite pattern, not a model of repentance.

Same name, different king. There are two Jehoahazes of significance: this 11th king of the divided northern kingdom (a Jehu-dynasty Israelite, c. 814-798 BC) and Jehoahaz son of Josiah, the 17th king of Judah, who was deposed by Pharaoh-Necho after a three-month reign and carried to Egypt (609 BC; 2 Kings 23:31-34). They lived two centuries apart in different kingdoms. Modern Bible reading sometimes conflates them; the text carefully distinguishes.

Besought the LORD and was given a deliverer (2 Kings 13:5).
Beseeching-without-turning: the chapter pattern that produced relief without reformation.

etymology: Hebrew Yehoash / Yoash (H3060 / H3101) — "Yahweh has bestowed" or "Yahweh-given." The longer and shorter forms refer to the same name; the same name was simultaneously borne by Joash of Judah (the eighth king of the southern kingdom, hidden in the temple by his aunt Jehosheba).
biblical_def: Jehoash of Israel (c. 798 — 782 BC), also called Joash, was the twelfth king of the divided northern kingdom (2 Kings 13:10-25; 2 Kings 14:8-16), son of Jehoahaz, third king of the Jehu dynasty, who reigned sixteen years and recovered the Israelite cities Hazael of Aram had taken from his father. His reign overlapped the final years of the prophet Elisha; the dying Elisha summoned him for the famous bow-and-arrows episode (2 Kings 13:14-19), in which Elisha had Joash shoot an arrow eastward (the 'arrow of the LORD's deliverance from Syria') and then strike the ground with the remaining arrows; Joash struck only three times and stopped, and Elisha grieved that he had not struck five or six times because his victory over Aram would now be limited to three. The prophecy was precisely fulfilled: Joash defeated Hazael's son Ben-Hadad three times and recovered the cities. Joash also captured King Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh after Amaziah's pride-driven challenge, broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, and carried the temple treasures to Samaria (2 Chr 25:23-24).
webster_summary: Twelfth king of Israel (c. 798-782 BC); son of Jehoahaz; reigned 16 years; recovered Israelite cities from Aram; received the bow-and-arrows prophecy from the dying Elisha (2 Kings 13:14-19); captured Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh.
webster_full: JEHOASH (JOASH) OF ISRAEL, proper noun. Hebrew Yehoash / Yoash (H3060 / H3101) — "Yahweh has bestowed."
Twelfth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 798-782 BC); son of Jehoahaz; third king of the Jehu dynasty.
16-year reign; recovered cities Hazael had taken from his father; defeated Aram three times under the dying Elisha's bow-and-arrows prophecy.
Captured King Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh; broke down 400 cubits of Jerusalem's wall; carried temple treasures to Samaria.
Distinct from Joash king of Judah (his contemporary; the boy-king hidden in the temple by Jehosheba).
scriptures: Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face... And Elisha said unto him, Take bow and arrows. And he took unto him bow and arrows. And he said to the king of Israel, Put thine hand upon the bow. And he put his hand upon it: and Elisha put his hands upon the king's hands. And he said, Open the window eastward... And he said, The arrow of the LORD's deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria.

And he said, Take the arrows. And he took them. And he said unto the king of Israel, Smite upon the ground. And he smote thrice, and stayed. And the man of God was wroth with him, and said, Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.

But Amaziah would not hear. Therefore Jehoash king of Israel went up; and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth-shemesh, which belongeth to Judah. And Judah was put to the worse before Israel; and they fled every man to their tents.

And Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah... at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem, and brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate, four hundred cubits. And he took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD, and in the treasures of the king's house...
corruption_summary: Jehoash of Israel is corrupted when he is confused with Joash of Judah (his exact contemporary with the same name in the rival kingdom), when the bow-and-arrows prophecy is read as merely picturesque rather than as a prophetic-conditional teaching on the relation between obedience and victory, or when his sack of Jerusalem is treated as merely military success rather than as covenant judgment on Amaziah's pride.
corruption_paragraphs: Two simultaneous Joashes. The Hebrew name Joash/Jehoash was simultaneously borne by the 8th king of Judah (the boy-king hidden by Jehosheba; 2 Kings 11-12) and the 12th king of Israel (this one). Modern readers sometimes confuse them. The narrator distinguishes carefully: Joash of Judah was a Davidic king of the southern kingdom; Jehoash of Israel was a Jehu-dynasty king of the northern kingdom; their reigns overlapped and they fought each other in person at Beth-shemesh (Jehoash captured and humiliated his Judean namesake's son Amaziah). Two kings; one name; opposite kingdoms.

Bow-and-arrows as picturesque. The dying Elisha's bow-and-arrows scene (2 Kings 13:14-19) is sometimes read as colorful prophet-theater. The chapter is teaching a serious doctrine: prophetic promise is conditional on the persistence and faith of those receiving it. Joash stopped striking the ground after three blows because he did not press in fully; the prophet's grief was theological. Half-hearted reception of God's offered grace produces half-hearted realization of God's offered deliverance. The same principle frames Matthew 13:58 ('he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief').

etymology: Hebrew Zekaryah (H2148) — "Yahweh has remembered." From zakar ("to remember") + Yah. The same Hebrew name was borne by 27 distinct biblical figures, most famously the post-exilic prophet Zechariah and the father of John the Baptist.
biblical_def: Zachariah of Israel (c. 753 — 752 BC) was the fourteenth king of the divided northern kingdom (2 Kings 14:29; 15:8-12), son of the great Jeroboam II and fifth and final king of the Jehu dynasty. His six-month reign was the last gasp of the longest-running dynasty in northern-kingdom history. He continued in Jeroboam's golden-calf apostasy and was publicly assassinated by Shallum the son of Jabesh in front of the people, ending the Jehu dynasty exactly four generations after Jehu had been promised by the LORD: 'thy sons shall sit on the throne of Israel unto the fourth generation' (2 Kings 10:30). The Chronicler's framing is deliberate: the promise was honored to the letter (Jehu — Jehoahaz — Joash — Jeroboam II — Zachariah, five names but four generations after Jehu); when the four-generation grant expired, the dynasty fell. His death began a 30-year period of chaotic political instability in the northern kingdom (six kings in 30 years, four of them assassinated) that ended with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC.
webster_summary: Fourteenth king of Israel (c. 753-752 BC); son of Jeroboam II; fifth and final king of the Jehu dynasty; reigned 6 months; assassinated publicly by Shallum son of Jabesh, fulfilling the 'four generations' promise to Jehu (2 Kings 10:30).
webster_full: ZACHARIAH (KING OF ISRAEL), proper noun. Hebrew Zekaryah (H2148) — "Yahweh has remembered," from zakar + Yah.
Fourteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 753-752 BC); son of Jeroboam II; fifth and final king of the Jehu dynasty.
Six-month reign; assassinated publicly by Shallum son of Jabesh (2 Kings 15:10).
His death fulfilled the LORD's promise to Jehu: 'thy sons shall sit on the throne of Israel unto the fourth generation' (2 Kings 10:30).
Distinct from Zechariah the post-exilic prophet, Zechariah father of John the Baptist (Luke 1), and at least 25 other biblical figures of the same name.
scriptures: In the thirty and eighth year of Azariah king of Judah did Zachariah the son of Jeroboam reign over Israel in Samaria six months. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done... And Shallum the son of Jabesh conspired against him, and smote him before the people, and slew him, and reigned in his stead.
2 Kings 15:12
This was the word of the LORD which he spake unto Jehu, saying, Thy sons shall sit on the throne of Israel unto the fourth generation. And so it came to pass.
2 Kings 10:30

And the LORD said unto Jehu, Because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes, and hast done unto the house of Ahab according to all that was in mine heart, thy children of the fourth generation shall sit on the throne of Israel.
Hosea 1:4-5

Call his name Jezreel; for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel. And it shall come to pass at that day, that I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel.
corruption_summary: Zachariah king of Israel is corrupted when he is confused with the post-exilic prophet Zechariah or the father of John the Baptist, when his six-month reign is treated merely as an end-of-dynasty footnote rather than as the precise fulfillment of the four-generation promise to Jehu, or when his assassination is read as random political chaos rather than as the unwinding of the Jehu-dynasty grant.
corruption_paragraphs: Multiple Zechariahs. The Hebrew name Zekaryah is one of the most common biblical names; it appears for at least 27 different figures across the Old Testament and into the New. The four most prominent: this king of Israel (2 Kings 15); the prophet Zechariah whose canonical book has 14 chapters (post-exilic, c. 520 BC); Zechariah son of Berechiah whom Jesus mentions in Matt 23:35 (possibly the same as the prophet, or possibly the priest of 2 Chr 24:20-22); and Zacharias the priest of the course of Abijah, father of John the Baptist (Luke 1:5-23). Modern readers commonly conflate these and merge their narratives. The text distinguishes; the dictionary follows the text.

Random-political-chaos misreading. The post-Zachariah period in Israel (753-722 BC) is sometimes presented as 30 years of meaningless palace coups under Assyrian pressure. The narrator's framing is precise: the LORD's four-generation grant to Jehu (2 Kings 10:30) expired exactly with Zachariah's death; from that point the dynastic stability of the northern kingdom was over, and what followed was the working-out of long-pronounced judgment. The chaos was not random; it was the unwinding of a covenant grant that had expired.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zekaryah (H2148) — "Yahweh has remembered," from zakar + Yah. Fourteenth king of Israel (c. 753-752 BC); fifth and final king of the Jehu dynasty.

His death was the precise fulfillment of the LORD's four-generation grant to Jehu.

etymology: Hebrew Shallum (H7967) — "retribution" or "recompense," from shalam ("to be complete, to repay"). Same root as shalom; the name carries an ironic edge in this king's brief and violent reign.
biblical_def: Shallum the son of Jabesh (c. 752 BC) was the fifteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15:10-15), assassin of Zachariah son of Jeroboam II (ending the Jehu dynasty), whose entire reign lasted only one month before he was himself assassinated by Menahem son of Gadi. His month-long reign is the shortest of any king named in the canonical record (shorter even than Zimri's seven days as a measurement, since seven days fit within one month). His name — 'retribution/recompense' — was prophetic of the immediate retributive coup against him. The episode demonstrates the political collapse of the northern kingdom in its last thirty years: the Jehu dynasty's expiration produced a period in which any military strongman could seize the throne briefly, and only the further violence of the next strongman could displace him. The northern kingdom from 752 to 722 BC saw six kings in thirty years, four of whom were assassinated. Shallum is the canonical pattern-piece of usurpation-without-mandate ending in immediate counter-usurpation.

Shallum the son of Jabesh began to reign in the nine and thirtieth year of Uzziah king of Judah; and he reigned a full month in Samaria. For Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, and came to Samaria, and smote Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria, and slew him, and reigned in his stead.

corruption_summary: Shallum is corrupted when his month-long reign is treated as a curiosity of brevity rather than as the canonical example of usurpation-without-mandate, when his name's irony ('retribution' carried by the man who killed his master and was killed in turn) is overlooked, or when he is conflated with the other biblical Shallums.
corruption_paragraphs: Brevity as curiosity. Shallum's one-month reign is sometimes treated merely as a Bible-trivia fact — the shortest reign in Scripture. The narrator's framing is theological. Hosea's contemporary commentary on the same period explains it: 'They have set up kings, but not by me' (Hos 8:4). The collapse of the post-Jehu-dynasty northern kingdom into rapid coup-after-coup demonstrates what happens to a political order that has been operating outside its prophetic mandate for a generation. Brevity is not curiosity; it is judgment.

Multiple Shallums. The Hebrew name Shallum was borne by at least eight distinct biblical figures, several of them post-exilic. The four most important: this king of Israel; Shallum the husband of the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:14); Shallum the priest-doorkeeper (1 Chr 9:17-19); and Shallum son of Naphtali (1 Chr 7:13). Some scholarly traditions also identify the Judean king Jehoahaz son of Josiah (carried to Egypt by Pharaoh-Necho) with a Shallum mentioned in Jer 22:11. The dictionary follows the text's careful distinctions.

etymology: Hebrew Menachem (H4505) — "comforter" or "consoler," from nacham ("to comfort, to console"). The same root produces Noah ('comfort, rest') and Nehemiah ('Yahweh comforts').
biblical_def: Menahem (c. 752 — 742 BC) was the sixteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15:14-22), military strongman from Tirzah who assassinated Shallum son of Jabesh after his one-month reign and ruled Israel for ten years. The Chronicler highlights two episodes. First, his brutal sack of the city of Tiphsah (or possibly Tappuah; manuscripts vary) and the surrounding region after they refused to open their gates to him: 'all the women therein that were with child he ripped up' (2 Kings 15:16) — a war crime by any standard, recorded in the canonical record as evidence of how thoroughly the northern kingdom had departed from Yahweh's law. Second, his tribute to Pul (Tiglath-Pileser III) king of Assyria: 'Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand. And Menahem exacted the money of Israel, even of all the mighty men of wealth, of each man fifty shekels of silver, to give to the king of Assyria' (2 Kings 15:19-20). The fifty-shekel-per-rich-man tax brought Israel formally under Assyrian vassalage for the first time, beginning the twenty-year slide that would end with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. The name 'comforter' is one of the most darkly ironic in the canonical record: under this king Israel was given neither comfort nor consolation. His reign appears in Tiglath-Pileser's own royal annals which name him as 'Menihimme of Samerina' — one of the few divided-monarchy kings attested in extant Assyrian inscriptions.
webster_summary: Sixteenth king of Israel (c. 752-742 BC); assassinated Shallum to take the throne; sacked Tiphsah with extreme brutality (ripping up pregnant women); paid 1,000 talents of silver tribute to Pul/Tiglath-Pileser III of Assyria, beginning Israel's vassalage to Assyria; attested in extant Assyrian royal annals as 'Menihimme of Samerina'.

corruption_summary: Menahem is corrupted when his Tiphsah brutality is treated as an isolated atrocity rather than as the canonical mirror of Hosea's prophetic word against Samaria (Hos 13:16), when his Assyrian tribute is read as merely political pragmatism, or when the irony of his name ('comforter') is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Tiphsah-as-isolated atrocity. The 'ripping up of pregnant women' at Tiphsah (2 Kings 15:16) is sometimes treated as a uniquely shocking war atrocity in the Bible. Hosea 13:16, prophesying against Samaria from within the same period, says precisely: 'their women with child shall be ripped up' — the same phrase, applied as covenant judgment to the kingdom whose king had committed it. The narrator and the prophet together make the point: a kingdom that practices this kind of warfare will receive it in judgment. The shock at Tiphsah is meant to make the reader feel the justice of Hos 13:16's announcement.

Tribute as pragmatism. 2 Kings 15:19-20's description of the 1,000-talent tribute and the 50-shekel-per-rich-man tax has sometimes been read as politically prudent — Menahem secured his throne by paying off the Assyrian superpower. The narrator's framing is theological: the tribute formalized Israel's vassalage to Assyria and began the twenty-year slide that ended with the fall of Samaria. Political pragmatism that purchases temporary safety by selling long-term covenant identity is a recurring biblical category of folly. Asa of Judah did the same with Ben-Hadad (1 Kings 15:18-19); Ahaz of Judah did the same with Tiglath-Pileser (2 Kings 16:7-9). All three ended badly.

etymology: Hebrew Peqachyah (H6494) — "Yahweh has opened (the eyes)" or "Yahweh-opened." From paqach ("to open the eyes") + Yah. The name's positive theological content sits ironically on a king whose eyes were closed to the very Yahweh his name confessed.
biblical_def: Pekahiah (c. 742 — 740 BC) was the seventeenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15:22-26), son of Menahem and only known successor to him. His two-year reign was the briefest possible stability in the chaotic post-Jehu period: he continued his father's golden-calf apostasy, continued his father's Assyrian-tribute policy, and was assassinated in the palace at Samaria by his own military commander Pekah son of Remaliah along with fifty Gileadite soldiers from his own bodyguard. The Chronicler's framing emphasizes the inside-job nature of the coup: 'Pekah the son of Remaliah, a captain of his, conspired against him, and smote him in Samaria, in the palace of the king's house, with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites: and he killed him, and reigned in his room' (2 Kings 15:25). Pekahiah's two-year reign and palace-coup death continued the pattern of usurpation-without-mandate that defined the northern kingdom's last thirty years. Six kings in thirty years (Zachariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, Hoshea); four of them assassinated.

corruption_summary: Pekahiah is corrupted when his two-year reign is treated as a forgettable interlude rather than as one more link in the divided-monarchy collapse chain, when his name's irony is overlooked, or when the Gileadite-conspiracy detail in the assassination is missed as evidence of the depth of palace disloyalty.
corruption_paragraphs: Forgettable-interlude misreading. Pekahiah's two-year reign sits between his more prominent father Menahem and his more prominent assassin Pekah. Many Bible surveys skip him entirely. The narrator's careful inclusion preserves the canonical evidence of the systematic collapse: six kings in thirty years was not random instability but the working-out of long-pronounced prophetic judgment (Hos 7:7; 8:4). Each individual reign matters because each link in the chain shows the same pattern.

Gileadite-conspiracy detail. 2 Kings 15:25 includes the specific detail that Pekah's conspiracy was carried out 'with Argob and Arieh, and with him fifty men of the Gileadites.' Argob and Arieh are otherwise unknown; the fifty Gileadites are revealing. Gilead was the trans-Jordanian region of Israel that had been the home territory of Jephthah and of the Tishbite Elijah; under the divided monarchy it had remained Israelite. The Gileadite participation in the palace coup against Pekahiah signals that even the most distant Israelite tribes had abandoned dynastic loyalty by this point. The kingdom's internal cohesion was gone.

etymology: Hebrew Peqach (H6492) — "open-eyed" or "watchful," from the same root paqach ("to open the eyes") that produced Pekahiah. The two king-names differ only in the divine-name suffix; the assassin's name dropped it.
biblical_def: Pekah (c. 740 — 732 BC) was the eighteenth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 15:25-31; 16:5-9; Isaiah 7), captain who assassinated Pekahiah son of Menahem and then aligned with Rezin king of Aram in the great Syro-Ephraimite anti-Assyrian coalition that produced the most theologically loaded crisis of the eighth-century OT. He reigned twenty years in some chronologies (the canonical figure; possibly inflated by including his earlier rebellion-period in Gilead before formally taking Samaria). The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 734-732 BC) was the campaign in which Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Aram allied to depose Ahaz of Judah and replace him with a puppet ('the son of Tabeel,' Isa 7:6) who would join their anti-Assyrian alliance. Isaiah's confrontation with Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool (Isa 7:1-25), the Immanuel prophecy, and Ahaz's fateful decision to bribe Tiglath-Pileser III for help against Pekah and Rezin all flow from this crisis. Tiglath-Pileser's response devastated Israel: he annexed Galilee, the Trans-Jordan, and the entire northern third of the kingdom, deporting the populations and reducing Israel to little more than the hill country of Ephraim around Samaria (2 Kings 15:29). The Israelite remnant then assassinated Pekah, and Hoshea son of Elah took the throne as the kingdom's final king. The Assyrian royal annals corroborate the deportation; Tiglath-Pileser claims Pekah's removal as his own action ('they overthrew Peqaha [Pekah] their king, and I placed Auaisi [Hoshea] over them').
webster_summary: Eighteenth king of Israel (c. 740-732 BC); assassinated Pekahiah; allied with Rezin of Aram in the Syro-Ephraimite War against Ahaz of Judah and Tiglath-Pileser III; the war that triggered Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy (Isa 7:14); Tiglath-Pileser annexed Galilee and Trans-Jordan and deported the populations; assassinated by Hoshea who took the throne.
webster_full: PEKAH, proper noun. Hebrew Peqach (H6492) — "open-eyed, watchful," from paqach.

Assassinated by Hoshea son of Elah who succeeded him; attested by name in Tiglath-Pileser's royal annals as 'Peqaha'.

corruption_summary: Pekah is corrupted when his Syro-Ephraimite coalition is read as merely regional politics rather than as the historical setting that occasioned Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy, when Isaiah's dismissive 'two tails of these smoking firebrands' is read as overconfidence rather than as covenant trust, or when his name's etymology (sharing a root with Pekahiah whom he assassinated) is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Syro-Ephraimite War as regional politics. The Pekah-Rezin alliance against Judah and Assyria is often presented in popular treatments as ordinary ancient Near Eastern coalition-building. The narrative's framing in Isaiah 7 makes it the historical setting for one of the most important christological prophecies in the Old Testament. Isaiah confronted Ahaz of Judah with the assurance that 'the two tails of these smoking firebrands' (Pekah and Rezin) would not depose him — if he would trust the LORD. Ahaz refused; Isaiah delivered the Immanuel prophecy anyway. The historical war is theologically inseparable from the Christological promise it occasioned.

Pekah and Pekahiah etymological-irony. The two king-names — Pekahiah (the assassinated) and Pekah (the assassin) — share the root paqach, 'to open the eyes.' The shorter form (Pekah) is the name of the man whose 'open eyes' saw an opportunity to kill his master. The longer Yah-suffixed form (Pekahiah) is the name of the man whose 'open eyes' should have seen Yahweh but did not. The Hebrew text intends this irony; English readers commonly miss it because the spelling-similarity is easier to read past than to read into.
